deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler's model in E260 treats fluid friction like solid (Amontons-type) friction. The frictional resistance on a tube wall is taken proportional to the local total pressure, p + l, where l is the atmospheric pressure expressed as a water height (about 30 ft). It is also proportional to perimeter/area, which for a tube of cross-section gg he writes as ~1/g. This makes the head along a tube vary exponentially. On the previous page (§54) Euler obtains, for a narrow tube BC of length b open at the bottom under a reservoir of head a: v = a + (g/α − l)(e^{αb/g} − 1), where v is the velocity head.

§55–56: put g = αl/n. Then v = a − ((n−1)/n) l (e^{nb/l} − 1). For b ≪ l this is ≈ a − (n−1)b, since e^{nb/l} − 1 ≈ nb/l. Flow is impossible when v ≤ 0.

This page:
- §56 (end), Experiment 1: shorten a long capillary until outflow just begins, and record its length b. At threshold a = (n−1)b, so n = (a+b)/b and α = ((a+b)/b)·(g/l).
- §57, Experiment 2: fix the length b and raise the head a until outflow begins. The same formula gives α.
- §58, Necessary condition: arrest of flow needs g < αl. If g > αl, the coefficient (g/α − l) is positive and v > 0 always. With the conjectured α = 1/4000 and l = 30 ft, the bound is g < 3/400 = 0.0075 ft. The diameter d of a circle of area g² is d = 2g/√π ≈ 1.128 g ≈ 0.0085 ft ≈ 1/118 ft, which Euler calls 'about one line'.
- §59: with a = 0 (a tube simply filled and held vertical), g ≤ αl gives v ≤ 0 for every length b, so nothing flows whatever the length. Euler proposes a third experiment: find the critical bore at which filled open tubes stop discharging; then α = g/l (completed on the next page).

The whole page serves to turn the pressure-dependent friction law into a measurable threshold, a 'yield' criterion, for determining α. On the next pages Euler infers from it that the retention depends on atmospheric pressure (it would fail in vacuo) and even links this to the electrical acceleration of efflux.
errors: §56: the printed formula reads α = (α+b)/b · g/l; the numerator must be a+b, as correctly printed in §57. This is a typographical error.
§58: printed 'deberet esse g > 3/400 ped.' should be g < 3/400 (immediately followed by the correct 'seu g < 0,0075'). Typo.

The approximation v ≈ a − (n−1)b uses e^{nb/l} − 1 ≈ nb/l. This requires nb ≪ l, which may not hold for large n (very thin tubes); the exact condition is a = ((n−1)/n) l (e^{nb/l} − 1). So the derived α is only approximate.

Physically, the whole threshold theory is wrong. Water retention in narrow open tubes is a capillary/surface-tension effect, independent of atmospheric pressure. Water has no pressure-proportional Coulomb wall friction, and steady Newtonian flow has no yield threshold. Euler's prediction that such tubes would empty in vacuo is false. 'One line' (1/144 ft) vs the computed 1/118 ft is only a rough agreement.

ideas.what: Critical-length / critical-head experiments to measure a friction coefficient from onset of flow
ideas.modern_name: Yield/threshold measurement (onset-of-flow test) for a pressure-dependent friction coefficient
ideas.usually_credited_to: Unsure; analogous wall-friction tests in granular mechanics (Jenike, 1960s)

ideas.what: Flow arrest whenever g < αl: pressure-proportional wall friction can hold a fluid column in a sufficiently narrow tube of any length
ideas.modern_name: Jamming/arching under Coulomb wall friction; Janssen-type saturation of pressure
ideas.usually_credited_to: Janssen (1895) for the exponential wall-friction column model in silos

ideas.what: Numerical estimate of the critical bore (~1/118 ft, about one line) from α = 1/4000, l = 30 ft
ideas.modern_name: Order-of-magnitude estimate of capillary length scale (misattributed to friction)

missed.claim: Euler's wall friction proportional to local pressure gives exponential pressure profiles along a column and a threshold of complete flow arrest independent of column length. This is mathematically the Janssen (1895) silo model plus a jamming criterion. It is not physical for water, but it is an early correct analysis of a Coulomb-frictional continuum in a tube. I am not aware that the granular-media literature credits Euler with this.
missed.quote: Si fuerit g=αl, seu g<αl, et a=0, tum si eiusmodi tubulus, cuiuscunque fuerit longitudinis, aqua impleatur, nihil ex eo effluet
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A historical footnote for granular mechanics: the model is 'wrong for fluids, right for grains'. Its value is historical rather than scientific.

deep.surprise_reason: The page derives a measurement protocol from an erroneous friction-proportional-to-pressure law. It is known in Truesdell's account of E260 as a failed theory. The only mildly interesting point is the unremarked formal anticipation of Janssen-type Coulomb wall friction and flow arrest.
transcription_corrections: §56 end: 'α=(α+b)/b·g/l' — the scan likewise appears to print α in the numerator; intended a+b (printing error, not a transcription error).
§58: 'g > 3/400 ped.' matches the print but is a printing error for g < 3/400.
§58: '85/10000' and '1/118' are consistent with the scan.
